[[SystemMessage(content='\n### Evidence Rules\nThese override every other instruction here.\n\n- A claim is grounded ONLY if it appears in a tool result returned during this\n  conversation. Do not answer from prior knowledge instead.\n- Never present a derived metric unless every input to it appears in a tool\n  result. Naming the formula does not make the output grounded.\n- If two sources conflict, report both with citations and say they conflict.\n\n### Know Your Tool\'s Limits\n- Your search tool returns short snippets and a machine-written summary. It will not surface deeper\n  content and wastes your budget. Locating the right filing does not mean you\n  can read it — if the figure is not in a snippet, it is NOT FOUND.\n- The summary/`answer` field is not a source. Use it only to decide which\n  underlying result to read; cite only URLs from the results list.\n- Judge relevance before using a result. A result about a different company,\n  filing, or year is not weak evidence — it is no evidence. Discard it.\n- Check each source\'s period against your assigned period. A source outside that\n  window is out of scope, not fresher data. Discard it, and never treat a\n  later-period document as a conflict with an in-period one.\n- Prefer primary sources (filings, company releases, official statistics) over\n  secondary coverage, and secondary over aggregators. Never treat forums,\n  sitemaps, or unrelated filings as sources. If, within budget, only a\n  secondary or aggregator source can supply a fact whose primary source you\n  correctly identified but could not extract, you may use it — but tag the\n  citation `[secondary-sourced]` or `[aggregator-sourced]` immediately after\n  it, so its lower reliability tier stays visible downstream. Our capital expenditures are typically difficult to project beyond the short-term given the number\n**Source**: https://ir.tesla.com/_flysystem/s3/sec/000162828026003952/tsla-20251231-gen.pdf\n\n    \n    ## Synthesized Summary***\n    Tesla’s 2024 cash‑flow picture shows a strong operating cash base but a sharp swing in discretionary spending that compressed free cash flow. Across the three quarters for which the filing provides quarterly detail (Q2‑24, Q3‑24 and Q4‑24), net cash provided by operating activities amounted to $3.6\u202fbillion, $6.3\u202fbillion and $4.8\u202fbillion respectively, for a cumulative $14.7\u202fbillion of operating cash flow in the period covered【https://ir.tesla.com/_flysystem/s3/sec/000162828025035738/tsla-20250723-gen.pdf】. During the same three‑quarter span, Tesla’s capital expenditures were $2.3\u202fbillion, $3.5\u202fbillion and $2.8\u202fbillion, totaling $8.6\u202fbillion, while free cash flow—defined as operating cash flow less capex—was $1.3\u202fbillion, $2.7\u202fbillion and $2.0\u202fbillion, or $6.1\u202fbillion in aggregate【https://ir.tesla.com/_flysystem/s3/sec/000162828025035738/tsla-20250723-gen.pdf】. The filing notes that free cash flow fell 89\u202f% year‑over‑year, indicating that 2024’s higher investment outlays and a modest slowdown in operating cash generation relative to 2023 materially compressed liquidity. By contrast, cash, cash equivalents and short‑term investments grew from $30.7\u202fbillion at the start of the period to $36.6\u202fbillion by the close of Q4‑24, reflecting the net effect of operating cash inflows exceeding the surge in capex. The data supplied does not include the corresponding 2023 quarterly figures, so a direct numeric comparison for FY\u202f2023 cannot be calculated from the provided documents. Nonetheless, the disclosed 89\u202f% YoY decline in free cash flow signals that 2024’s cash generation was markedly less resilient than the prior year, driven primarily by elevated capex tied to new gigafactory build‑outs and the rollout of robotaxi services.\n    ', name='company_ir_search', tool_call_id='call_423050'), AIMessage(content=[], additional_kwargs={'function_call': {'name': Isah | Medium\n**Content**: # **Tesla Full Year 2024 Analysis — A Review of Actual Performance & My Financial Forecast**. Now that the Company’s Full-Year 2024 financials are available, In this article, I will be reviewing my analysis and give some context to Tesla’s performance in 2024 plus what to look out for from the company in 2025. Tesla had an 18.4% automotive gross profit margin (including regulatory credits) in 2024 and 23.3% in 2023 as automotive revenues declined by 6% to $77 billion from $82.4 billion year-on-year. The Tesla Energy segment’s revenues rose 67% to $10 billion in 2024 from $6 billion in 2023, while its gross profit margin rose slightly to 26.2% from 23.3%. Tesla Services and Other had a 5.8% gross profit margin in 2024, down from 6.2% in 2023. Segment revenues rose 27% to $10.5 billion in 2024 from $8.3 billion in 2023. Tesla’s revenue rose by only 1% to $97.6 billion in 2024 from $96.7 billion in 2023.\n**Source**: https://medium.com/@nambos3rd/tesla-full-year-2024-analysis-a-review-of-actual-performance-my-financial-forecast-41ee70091b5a\n\n\n# Result 5\n**Title**: Form 10-K\n**Content**: | x | **ANNUAL REPORT PURSUANT TO SECTION 13 OR 15(d) OF THE SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934** |. | ¨ | **TRANSITION REPORT PURSUANT TO SECTION 13 OR 15(d) OF THE SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934** |. The 2025 Form\u202f10‑K filing notes that capital expenditures for FY\u202f2024 are projected to exceed $20\u202fbillion, reflecting the scale of investments in vehicle production capacity, battery megafactories and new technologies【https://ir.tesla.com/_flysystem/s3/sec/000162828026003952/tsla-20251231-gen.pdf】. Free cash flow (FCF) is the cash a company has left after spending money to support and maintain its operations and capital assets. ## What Is Free Cash Flow (FCF)? Free cash flow (FCF) is the amount of cash\xa0that a company has left after accounting for spending on operations and capital asset maintenance. Unlike other measures that are used to analyze cash flow in a company, such as earnings or net income, free cash flow excludes the non-cash expenses of the company's income statement. A cash flow statement is a tool that tracks a company's cash inflows and outflows to help evaluate its liquidity and financial stability. Cash Flow Statement:max_bytes(150000):strip_icc():format(webp)/cashflowstatement-recirc-blue-777721714b8f49a5b5103337a8510653.jpg). ## What Is a Cash Flow Statement? A cash flow statement is a financial\xa0statement that\xa0reflects how much cash comes in and out of a business over a certain period. It is one of the most intuitive financial statements because it follows the cash earned by the business through operating, investment, and financing activities. Cash flow statements highlight a company's financial well-being based on its cash inflows and outflows. Inflows are the result of a company's ongoing operations and external investment sources, while outflows reflect money paid for business activities and investments during a given period. Profitable companies can fail to adequately manage cash flow, which is why the cash flow statement is important for investors and analysts. Free cash flow is the amount of cash flow left over after all cash operating expenses, including capex spending and net changes in working capital, that is free to spend on dividends, buybacks, acquisitions and debt reduction. This year Microsoft is likely to generate about $69.9 billion in FCF based on analyst revenue estimates and using the company's guidance on its capex spending. Moreover, based on estimates from a survey of 52 analysts, revenue for the year ending June 30, 2024 is forecast to rise by 15.2% from $211.9 billion last year to $244.3 billion.\n**Source**: https://finance.yahoo.com/news/microsofts-free-cash-flow-could-140002170.html\n\n\n# Result 2\n**Title**: FY24 Q1 - The same guidance implies that capex (the cash outlays for property, plant, equipment and related acquisitions) was expected to be in the low‑double‑digit‑billion‑dollar range; the FY24\u202fQ1 cash‑flow statement shows a quarterly acquisition‑related outflow of about\u202f$1.19\u202fbillion, suggesting an annualized capex level of roughly\u202f$4½–$5\u202fbillion, while the broader guidance used in the free‑cash‑flow estimate points to a total FY24 capex of roughly $12\u202fbillion (the difference between operating cash flow and free cash flow).  Because free cash flow equals operating cash flow minus capex, the implied operating cash flow for FY24 would be in the vicinity of $80\u202fbillion. Unpack the mechanics of Meta Platforms' free cash flow, examining its unique generation drivers and strategic allocation for growth and shareholder value. Free Cash Flow (FCF) is a paramount financial metric for evaluating the true economic power of large technology enterprises like Meta Platforms, Inc. The metric represents the actual discretionary cash a company generates after covering the costs necessary to maintain and expand its operational assets. Investors consider FCF a more reliable indicator of financial health than Net Income because it strips away non-cash accounting complexities, reflecting pure liquidity. ## Defining Free Cash Flow for Meta Platforms. Free Cash Flow is the capital remaining after a company pays for its operating expenses and Capital Expenditures (CapEx). Net Income can be skewed by non-cash charges such as depreciation, amortization, and Stock-Based Compensation. FCF, derived from the Statement of Cash Flows, adjusts for these non-cash items, providing a truer measure of the cash available to the business. ## The Calculation of Meta’s Free Cash Flow. The standard calculation for Free Cash Flow is Operating Cash Flow (OCF) minus Capital Expenditures (CapEx). OCF represents the cash generated from the company’s normal business activities, such as advertising revenue, after paying for operating expenses. To calculate OCF, Net Income is the starting point, adjusted for non-cash expenses and changes in working capital. Meta’s OCF is substantial, driven by its high-margin advertising business and large non-cash add-backs. Meta’s CapEx is the differentiator between its high OCF and its final FCF figure. ## Specific Drivers of Meta’s Operating Cash Flow. Meta’s Operating Cash Flow is significantly boosted by the accounting treatment of specific non-cash expenses. The consistent and large contributions from SBC and D&A remain the dominant structural drivers that make Meta’s OCF consistently higher than its Net Income. ## How Meta Deploys Its Free Cash Flow. The considerable Free Cash Flow generated by Meta Platforms is systematically deployed across multiple channels, with a primary focus on returning capital to shareholders. In a strategic shift, Meta initiated a quarterly cash dividend in 2024, marking its transition into a more mature technology company.\n**Source**: https://legalclarity.org/how-meta-platforms-generates-and-uses-free-cash-flow\n\n\n# Result 5\n**Title**: Depreciation & Amortization - Meta Platforms, Inc. NVIDIA’s cash-flow profile has shifted from “strong but cyclical semiconductor cash generation” to a **hyper–cash-generative platform phase**: FY2025 operating cash flow was **$64.089B** vs **$28.090B** in FY2024 (both USD), alongside an aggressive ramp in shareholder returns (repurchases) and a large increase in balance-sheet liquidity (cash + marketable securities). Looking forward, the most important cash-flow swing factors are (1) **working-capital intensity** tied to supply/capacity commitments and annual architecture transitions, and (2) **geopolitical/export-control volatility** that can cause inventory provisions/obsolescence and force product redesigns—both explicitly highlighted risks in filings. NVIDIA’s liquidity (cash + marketable securities) increased materially from FY2024 to FY2025. * **Scale/operating leverage feeding CFO:** The company directly links higher FY2025 operating cash flow to revenue growth, which—given NVIDIA’s high gross margin profile in the current cycle—typically translates into strong cash conversion. * **Cash earnings financing capital return:** FY2025 cash generation was large enough to fund very significant repurchases without meaningfully depleting cash (because they also expanded marketable securities). NVIDIA is using cash primarily for (1) **repurchases**, (2) **dividends**, while maintaining ample liquidity and continuing investment in supply/capacity and infrastructure. **Cash-flow implication:** if demand remains strong and supply ramps smoothly, CFO stays robust because (i) earnings remain high, and (ii) working-capital investments are “absorbed” by margin dollars. ### B) The biggest cash-flow risk: supply/capacity commitments + faster product cadence. **Cash-flow implication:** even with strong demand, CFO volatility can rise due to:. **Cash-flow implication:** NVIDIA is effectively locking in future cash outflows to secure capacity and support offerings (e.g., DGX Cloud), which can protect revenue growth but increases fixed commitments if demand softens or mix shifts. If NVIDIA sustains its current demand environment while executing its faster annual architecture cadence, **CFO likely remains structurally high**—and the company has already set up the balance sheet (marketable securities) and capital-return machinery (large repurchase authorization) to deploy that cash. The principal risks to future cash compounding are **not** traditional leverage/liquidity constraints (they explicitly state sufficient liquidity), but rather (1) **working-capital/commitment rigidity** if demand timing shifts, and (2) **export-control shocks** that can strand inventory and force redesigns—both clearly emphasized in the filings.\n**Source**: https://alpha-analyst.com/insights/nvidia-cash-flow-analysis-fy2025-surge-risks-outlook\n\n\n# Result 4\n**Title**: Electronic Arts FY2025 Q2 Earnings Release - InvestGame.net\n**Content**: Subscribe for our weekly newsletter. # Electronic Arts FY2025 Q2 Earnings Release.
